title: Linking simple clauses: cumulative review
objectives: Connect simple clauses using and, but, because and so.
Distinguish a reason from a result.
Review selected A2 grammar in connected sentences.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A clause is a group of words that usually includes a subject and a verb. We can connect simple clauses to show how ideas are related. ‘I was tired, but I finished my work’ links two ideas that contrast. ‘I was tired, so I went to bed’ links a situation with its result.

In this unit, use and to add an idea, but to show a contrast, because to give a reason, and so to introduce a result. The relationship between ideas guides the choice. This unit also reviews earlier grammar, including past forms, future plans, comparisons and time expressions.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Use and to connect related ideas: ‘Mia opened the door, and Ben came in’. Use but when the second idea contrasts with the first: ‘The room is small, but it is comfortable’. Use because before a reason: ‘I stayed at home because I was ill’. Use so before a result: ‘I was ill, so I stayed at home’.

Both parts of these examples have a subject and verb. The words can also connect other grammatical structures, but here we focus on simple clauses. In writing, a comma often appears before and, but or so when they connect two full clauses, especially when that makes the sentence easier to read. A comma is not normally needed before because in these simple examples.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘I took an umbrella because it was raining’ with ‘It was raining, so I took an umbrella’. The facts are similar, but the order of reason and result changes. Because introduces the reason; so introduces the result. You can put a because clause first: ‘Because it was raining, I took an umbrella’. A comma commonly follows an opening because clause.

Read the examples below. ‘And’ can add an action in a sequence: ‘She stood up and opened the door’. ‘But’ can contrast an expectation and a fact: ‘It was cold, but we enjoyed the walk’. The linking word does not change the tense by itself; choose each verb form from its meaning and time.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use because and so together to connect the same reason and result in one sentence: use ‘Because I was tired, I went home’ or ‘I was tired, so I went home’. The sentence ‘Because I was tired, so I went home’ is not standard English.

And does not automatically mean that the second event was caused by the first; use because or so when you need to make a reason or result clear. In real communication, more than one connector may sometimes be possible with a different emphasis. In an exercise, use the relationship stated in the context.

examples.sentence: I made tea, and Sam made coffee.
The room is small, but it is comfortable.
I stayed home because I was ill.
It was raining, so we took a taxi.
Because it was late, we left.
examples.note: A because clause can come first.

examples.sentence: She stood up and opened the door.
examples.note: And links actions in a sequence.

examples.sentence: I was tired, but I finished my homework.
We are going to eat at home because the café is closed.
examples.note: The future plan and the reason are linked with because.

common_errors.incorrect: Because I was tired, so I went home.
common_errors.correct: Because I was tired, I went home.
common_errors.reason: Do not use because and so together for the same connection.

common_errors.incorrect: I stayed home so I was ill.
common_errors.correct: I stayed home because I was ill.

common_errors.incorrect: It was raining, because we took a taxi.
common_errors.correct: It was raining, so we took a taxi.

summary: Use and to add ideas and but to show contrast.
Use because before a reason and so before a result.
Choose the verb tense from the meaning; the connector does not determine it by itself.

exercises.prompt: I was tired, ___ I finished the report. The second idea contrasts with the first.
exercises.explanation: But introduces the stated contrast.

option_feedback.a: “but” fits here. But introduces the stated contrast.
option_feedback.b: “because” does not fit here. But introduces the stated contrast.
option_feedback.c: “so” does not fit here. But introduces the stated contrast.
option_feedback.d: “for” does not fit here. But introduces the stated contrast.

option_feedback.b: “because” fits here. Because introduces the reason it was cold.
option_feedback.c: “but” does not fit here. Because introduces the reason it was cold.
option_feedback.d: “than” does not fit here. Because introduces the reason it was cold.

exercises.prompt: At six yesterday, I ___ dinner when the phone rang.
exercises.explanation: Was cooking describes the past action in progress.

option_feedback.a: “cook” does not fit here. Was cooking describes the past action in progress.
option_feedback.b: “am cooking” does not fit here. Was cooking describes the past action in progress.
option_feedback.c: “will cooking” does not fit here. Was cooking describes the past action in progress.
option_feedback.d: “was cooking” fits here. Was cooking describes the past action in progress.

exercises.prompt: I think it ___ tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Use will plus the base verb for this prediction.

option_feedback.a: “rains yesterday” does not fit here. Use will plus the base verb for this prediction.
option_feedback.b: “will rains” does not fit here. Use will plus the base verb for this prediction.
option_feedback.c: “will rain” fits here. Use will plus the base verb for this prediction.
option_feedback.d: “will to rain” does not fit here. Use will plus the base verb for this prediction.

exercises.prompt: It was cold, ___ I wore a coat. Introduce the result.
exercises.explanation: So introduces the result.

exercises.prompt: I wore a coat ___ it was cold. Introduce the reason.
exercises.explanation: Because introduces the reason.

exercises.prompt: The bag is small, ___ it is heavy. Show a contrast.
exercises.explanation: But introduces the contrast.

exercises.prompt: I opened the book ___ read the first page. Add the next action.
exercises.explanation: And adds an action.

exercises.prompt: At nine yesterday, we ___ studying. Use the positive past form of be.
exercises.explanation: We takes were in the past continuous.

exercises.prompt: She is going to ___ tomorrow. (travel)
exercises.explanation: Use the base verb after going to.

exercises.prompt: This is the ___ room in the house. (large)
exercises.explanation: Largest is the superlative of large.

exercises.explanation: Use on with a named day.
